where: noun row, beside חֶסֶד and θεός; 'Spirit of truth' phrases
why: אֱמֶת (reliability, faithfulness) and ἀλήθεια (what is real or correct) are pooled in one noun form, so the page can read as equating the Hebrew and Greek senses; 'the Spirit of truth' rows stand close to disputes about the Spirit's procession.
how_to_keep_level: Keep each phrase as written ('steadfast love and truth', 'the Spirit of truth'), show Hebrew and Greek words as separate labelled sub-rows, and add no gloss on what the Spirit's relation to the Father or Son is.

where: noun row beside πίστις ('faith working through love', 'faith, hope and love') and the verb rows (Father loves the Son; love one another / love your enemies)
why: Placing love beside faith can read as saying love completes or forms faith (Catholic, Orthodox) or only follows from it (Lutheran, Reformed); and grouping God's love for the Son, for the world and for the elect-language rows together can look like a view on whom God loves.
how_to_keep_level: Set 'faith working through love' and similar phrases side by side with the plain 'God so loved the world' and 'chosen/beloved' rows, kept as written, and do not order the rows to suggest a priority between love and faith.

where: noun row ('the righteousness of God', 'righteousness by/from faith', 'justice and righteousness'); the pooling of צֶדֶק/צְדָקָה with δικαιοσύνη; the pairing with מִשְׁפָּט and עָשָׂה
why: 'The righteousness of God' is exactly where the readers part (God's own saving justice, a status given to the believer, or an infused quality), and a row set beside 'by faith' or beside 'doing righteousness' will tilt toward one side; the Hebrew words also carry justice and the covenant faithfulness a Jewish reader hears, which the English 'righteousness' flattens.
how_to_keep_level: Keep 'the righteousness of God' as one row with no gloss on whose righteousness it is; put the 'by faith' rows and the 'doing righteousness / justice' rows side by side in the same list rather than apart; label the Hebrew rows as Hebrew and let 'justice' and 'righteousness' appear as the BSB gives them.

where: noun row beside διά and ἐκ ('through faith', 'by faith', 'of faith'); πίστις (belief or faithfulness) pooled with the verb πιστεύω (believe); beside ἀγάπη and ἔχω
why: Whether πίστις is trust, belief or faithfulness, whether 'faith of Christ' is faith in him or his faithfulness, and how faith stands to works are the points where the readers divide; splitting 'justified by faith' from James on works, or gathering belief and faithfulness under one noun, picks a side.
how_to_keep_level: Keep each phrase as the BSB reads it, with 'faith in Christ' and 'faithfulness of Christ' readings not resolved; place the Pauline 'by faith' rows and the James 'faith without works' rows side by side in one list; give the noun and the verb as separate forms and do not state that they are the same thing.

where: noun row beside δίδωμι ('grace given'), κατά, and θεός/Χριστός/Ἰησοῦς; the greeting formulas 'grace and peace'
why: Grace as a gift received at baptism or in the sacraments, as prevenient and resistible, as irresistible, or as the uncreated energies of God are all read onto the same verses; a 'grace given' row may seem to say how grace is conveyed. Only χάρις is listed, so the Hebrew חֵן and the idea of favour are absent, which a Jewish reader may notice.
how_to_keep_level: Keep the phrases ('grace given to me', 'by grace you have been saved', 'the grace of our Lord') as written, add no row on how or when grace is received, and keep the greeting rows apart from the rows that say what grace does.

where: noun row (ἔλεος only), beside εἰρήνη, κύριος, πατήρ ('grace, mercy and peace')
why: Only the Greek word is listed, so the Hebrew חֶסֶד (which the Septuagint renders with ἔλεος) is not here and appears under love and truth; a reader may take the hub to be complete when it is Greek-only. Mercy as an act of charity (the works of mercy) is also a Catholic and Orthodox emphasis not in the grouping.
how_to_keep_level: Say plainly that the hub is the Greek word, keep the phrases as written, and link out to the Hebrew steadfast-love rows rather than merging them.

where: noun row beside δόξα ('hope of glory'), Χριστός, θεός; the Hebrew group (מִקְוֶה, תִּקְוָה, תּוֹחֶלֶת) pooled with ἐλπίς; the verb row with odd subjects (Paul, Herod, 'nations')
why: 'The hope of Israel' and 'the hope of the gospel' will be read as one hope (the church fulfils Israel) or as two (dispensational and Jewish readers), and a single noun row can silently choose; the Hebrew words are partly 'expectation, waiting' and partly 'a cord, a pool,' so pooling them with ἐλπίς overstates equivalence.
how_to_keep_level: Keep 'the hope of Israel', 'the hope of glory', 'the hope of the resurrection' each as written and in their own rows side by side; mark Hebrew and Greek separately; leave out any row that implies who the hope belongs to.

where: adjective row (ἅγιος only): 'holy' used of the Spirit, of saints/people, of God, of things; no Hebrew קָדוֹשׁ
why: ἅγιος covers 'Holy Spirit', 'the saints' and 'holy' as a quality, so the verse list for holiness is mostly the Spirit's title, which misleads; and how the saints come to be holy (positional, imputed, a crisis, or a process of growth) is what Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox readers argue.
how_to_keep_level: Split the rows by who or what is called holy (the Spirit, God, people, places and things) and keep 'saints' phrases as written; do not present 'holy Spirit' verses as verses about holiness; say the hub is the Greek word and link the Hebrew to its own list.

where: noun row beside θεός, יהוה, Χριστός, Ἰησοῦς ('the glory of the LORD', 'the glory of Christ'); δόξα (opinion, splendour) pooled with כָּבוֹד (weight) and הֶדֶר
why: Putting 'the glory of the LORD' and 'the glory of Christ' in one row can look like asserting they are the same glory, which Trinitarian readers accept and others weigh differently; the Orthodox hear glory as uncreated light, the Jewish reader as the kavod that dwelt in the Temple, and the English word covers both.
how_to_keep_level: Keep the phrases as written and in separate rows ('the glory of the LORD', 'the glory of Christ'), do not combine them into one, and label the Hebrew and Greek words as different words.

where: noun row beside χάρις, θεός, ἔλεος, עַם, אֱמֶת ('peace and truth'); שָׁלוֹם and εἰρήνη pooled with שַׁלְוָה (calm)
why: Shalom (wholeness, the well-being of a people) and eirene (peace, the absence of conflict, peace with God) are pooled, and 'peace with God' is read by some as a justification statement and by others as relation to God; the hub could be taken to reduce peace to inner peace or to a political peace.
how_to_keep_level: Keep phrases as written, put 'peace with God', 'peace on earth' and the greeting formulas as separate rows, and say nothing about the sort of peace a row means.

where: noun row beside πληρόω ('filled with joy'), μετά, ἐπί; six Hebrew nouns pooled with χαρά
why: 'Joy in the Holy Spirit' and rows on shouting or exultation may be read as Pentecostal-leaning if grouped, and the Hebrew words span gladness, rejoicing and festival, which the English 'joy' flattens.
how_to_keep_level: Keep the phrases as written, do not set rows on the Spirit's joy apart from the others, and show the Hebrew and Greek as separate sub-rows.

where: verb row (יהוה -> -, '-> ἁμαρτία', 'πυρετός -> αὐτός'); ἀφίημι pooled with סָלַח; noun row beside μετάνοια, κηρύσσω, ἄφεσις ('repentance and forgiveness of sins')
why: ἀφίημι also means 'leave, let go, permit', and the profile shows 'the fever left her' in the verb group, so the page would list non-forgiveness verses as forgiveness; who may forgive (God alone, or through priestly absolution in John 20:23), whether forgiveness is conditional on repentance, and 'forgive us as we forgive' are all contested, and the Hebrew סָלַח is used only of God, unlike the Greek.
how_to_keep_level: Remove the verses where ἀφίημι does not mean forgive, keep rows by who forgives and what is forgiven as written, and set 'repentance for the forgiveness of sins', 'forgive us as we forgive' and John 20:23 side by side without ordering them or stating a condition.

where: verb row (שׁוּב: 1,024 verses with subjects such as הוּא, בֵּן, אִישׁ, יָד); noun row beside βάπτισμα, ἄφεσις, ἁμαρτία ('a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins')
why: שׁוּב simply means 'turn, return', so most of its 1,024 verses are about returning or going back and not repentance, which would make the hub's verse list false; and grouping repentance beside baptism and forgiveness decides a point (baptismal regeneration, sacramental penance, or repentance as a prior condition) on which these readers divide. The Hebrew teshuvah is also a Jewish concept in its own right.
how_to_keep_level: Limit the Hebrew rows to the verses where the BSB translates שׁוּב as repent or turn from sin, and give the other uses of שׁוּב their own list; keep 'baptism of repentance' as one phrase as written and side by side with the 'repent and turn' rows, with no ordering of repentance, baptism and forgiveness.

where: verb rows (Ἰησοῦς, μαθητής, עַם 'prays'); noun row beside שָׁמַע, תְּחִנָּה ('hear my prayer')
why: Prayer to saints and the Virgin, set prayers and liturgy, and prayer in tongues are not in the grouping but a reader may look for them; פָּלַל also means 'to intercede, to judge', so the Hebrew verb is not only prayer.
how_to_keep_level: Keep the rows by who prays and to whom as the text reads, add no row on any practice not in the text, and note that פָּלַל has a wider range of uses.

where: noun row beside יהוה, δόξα, יָדָה ('thank, confess'), שֵׁם, Χριστός; הָלַל (a verb, 'to praise') listed under the noun form
why: Praise, thanksgiving, worship and confession are pooled across Hebrew words, and a hub on 'praise' can read as taking sides on worship style (raised hands, set liturgy, hymns); rows where Christ receives praise are read as a statement on his divinity by some and not by others.
how_to_keep_level: Keep the phrases as written, keep 'praise', 'thanks' and 'worship' as separate rows, and do not group rows by where or how the praise is offered.
